meta.title: OTCA practice question bank
meta.note: answer is a 0-based index into options. Add your own questions freely.

questions.q: What best distinguishes observability from monitoring?
options: Observability uses dashboards; monitoring uses alerts
Observability lets you ask new, unanticipated questions from system outputs; monitoring answers predefined questions
Observability applies only to Kubernetes; monitoring applies to VMs
Monitoring collects traces; observability collects metrics
questions.explain: Monitoring answers known questions; observability lets you explore unknown-unknowns without redeploying.

questions.q: Which of the following does the OpenTelemetry project deliberately NOT provide?
options: A storage backend and visualization UI
questions.explain: OTel generates, collects, processes and exports telemetry; storage, querying and dashboards are left to backends like Prometheus, Jaeger, Grafana or vendors.

questions.q: OpenTelemetry was created in 2019 by merging which two projects?
questions.explain: OpenTracing + OpenCensus merged into OpenTelemetry under the CNCF in 2019.

questions.q: Which signal is best suited for following a single request across multiple microservices?
questions.explain: Traces capture the causal, cross-service path of one request. Metrics aggregate; logs are local detail; baggage is context, not a signal.

questions.q: Which signal is currently experimental / still in development in OpenTelemetry?
questions.explain: Profiles are the emerging fourth signal. Traces, metrics and the logs data model/SDK are stable.

questions.q: What is an exemplar?
options: A sample data point on a metric carrying a TraceId/SpanId that links to a representative trace
A reference implementation of the API
A required attribute in semantic conventions
questions.explain: Exemplars are the metrics-to-traces bridge: from a latency spike on a chart straight into a slow trace.

questions.q: A team records the raw user ID as an attribute on a request-count metric. Most likely consequence?
options: A cardinality explosion: one time series per user, driving up backend cost
questions.explain: Each unique attribute combination is a separate time series. Remedies: SDK Views or Collector transform/attributes processors.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of semantic conventions?
options: Standardize attribute names/values so any backend or tool can interpret telemetry uniformly
questions.explain: A shared vocabulary (http.request.method, service.name...) enables portable dashboards and OTel-aware processing.

questions.q: The strongest strategy for correlating a log line with the request that produced it is:
options: Stamping the log record with the active span's TraceId/SpanId
Matching log text against span names
questions.explain: Identity beats time: logs emitted inside an active span get exact trace/span IDs.

questions.q: Which value proposition is central to OpenTelemetry?
options: It replaces the need for observability backends
Instrument once, export to any compatible backend - no vendor lock-in at the instrumentation layer
It guarantees 100% sampling with zero overhead
It only works with CNCF backends
questions.explain: Vendor neutrality: swap backends without re-instrumenting your code.

questions.q: High-cardinality data such as request IDs and full URLs is best placed on:
questions.explain: Spans and logs tolerate high cardinality (they are sampled/filtered); metrics do not. Resource attributes describe the producer.

questions.q: The RED method tracks which three things per service?
questions.explain: RED = request Rate, Error rate, Duration - typically derived from spans or HTTP histograms. USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) covers resources.

questions.q: Which backend is a typical destination for TRACES exported from OpenTelemetry?
questions.explain: Jaeger (and Tempo, Zipkin) store traces; Prometheus stores metrics; Loki stores logs. Grafana visualizes all of them.

questions.q: Baggage is best described as:
options: Cross-cutting key/value context propagated with a request, separate from the signals
questions.explain: Baggage is propagated context, not a signal - and it is not automatically attached to any telemetry.

questions.q: What is OpenTelemetry's status within the CNCF?
questions.explain: OTel is a CNCF incubating project and one of the most active CNCF projects, second only to Kubernetes by contributors.

questions.q: Why are the OpenTelemetry API and SDK separate?
options: So library authors can instrument against the API with zero runtime cost when no SDK is configured - API calls become no-ops
Because the API is written in Go
questions.explain: Without a registered SDK the API is a no-op with negligible cost. A recurring exam theme.

questions.q: Which dependency should a shared open-source library declare to add OTel instrumentation?
questions.explain: Libraries depend on the API only; the application decides whether to wire in an SDK.

questions.q: What are the sizes of a TraceId and a SpanId?
questions.explain: TraceId = 16 bytes (32 hex chars); SpanId = 8 bytes (16 hex chars).

questions.q: Which span kind should an HTTP service handling an inbound request use?
questions.explain: SERVER for inbound remote calls, CLIENT for outbound, PRODUCER/CONSUMER for messaging, INTERNAL otherwise.

questions.q: A server span for a request that returned HTTP 404 should have status:
options: UNSET - 4xx does not automatically mark a server span as error
questions.explain: By convention 5xx sets ERROR on server spans; 4xx does not (the server behaved correctly). On CLIENT spans 4xx is an error.

questions.q: A consumer processes one batch containing messages from 50 different producer traces. How should its span reference them?
options: Span links to the producer spans
questions.explain: Span links express causal relations that are not parent-child - the canonical batch/fan-in case. A span has at most one parent.

questions.q: Which is a good span name?
questions.explain: Span names must be low-cardinality templates; concrete URLs and IDs go into attributes such as url.full.

questions.q: Which instrument fits 'number of items currently in a queue' (goes up and down, additive)?
questions.explain: Additive but can decrease -> UpDownCounter. Counter is monotonic-only.

questions.q: Which instrument fits 'CPU temperature', where summing values across sensors is meaningless?
questions.explain: Use a Gauge precisely when addition makes no sense - a non-additive sampled value.

questions.q: Which instrument should record HTTP request duration so percentiles can be computed?
questions.explain: Histograms capture the distribution, enabling percentiles/heatmaps and (with exemplars) trace drill-down.

questions.q: How do asynchronous (observable) instruments report values?
options: The app calls add()/record() on every event
Via a callback the SDK invokes at each collection cycle
They are pushed by the Collector
questions.explain: Observable instruments register callbacks read at collection time - ideal for values you read on demand (CPU, queue depth).

questions.q: Prometheus as a backend requires which metric temporality?
questions.explain: Prometheus's model is cumulative. Temporality is configured per exporter; several SaaS backends prefer delta.

questions.q: The primary SDK tool for dropping a high-cardinality attribute from one metric without changing recording code is:
questions.explain: A View selects an instrument and can allow-list attribute keys, change aggregation, rename, or drop the stream entirely.

questions.q: What is the recommended way for an application to emit OpenTelemetry logs?
options: Replace the logging library with direct Logs Bridge API calls everywhere
Keep the existing logger and attach an OTel appender/bridge that forwards records into the LoggerProvider
Send syslog directly to the backend
questions.explain: The bridge model: keep log4j/logback/slog/etc.; OTel forwards and enriches its records. The Bridge API is for appender authors.

questions.q: A LogRecord has severity_number 17. Which severity block is that?
questions.explain: Blocks of four: TRACE 1-4, DEBUG 5-8, INFO 9-12, WARN 13-16, ERROR 17-20, FATAL 21-24.

questions.q: Logs reach the backend but carry no trace IDs although requests are traced. Most likely cause?
options: The OTel log appender/bridge is not installed, or the logs are emitted outside an active span
The traceparent header is too long
questions.explain: Correlation requires the bridge plus an active span in context at emit time.

questions.q: What does a Resource describe?
options: The immutable identity of the telemetry producer (service, host, pod, cloud), attached to all signals
questions.explain: The Resource is what makes signals from one workload correlatable; service.name is its most critical key.

questions.q: Which environment variable sets service.name?
questions.explain: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME - it also overrides a service.name given inside OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES.

questions.q: What are OpenTelemetry's default context propagators?
options: W3C Trace Context and W3C Baggage
questions.explain: Defaults: traceparent/tracestate + the baggage header. B3, Jaeger and X-Ray are opt-in via OTEL_PROPAGATORS.

questions.q: In traceparent: 00-4bf9...4736-00f0...02b7-01, what does the trailing 01 mean?
questions.explain: The last field is the flags byte; 01 = sampled bit set, carrying the head-sampling decision downstream.

questions.q: Service A (tracecontext) calls service B configured with only the B3 propagator. Result?
options: The trace breaks: B cannot extract A's context and starts a new trace
questions.explain: Propagator mismatch is the #1 cause of broken traces. Fix by listing both formats on both sides (OTEL_PROPAGATORS=tracecontext,baggage,b3).

questions.q: What is Baggage for?
options: Propagating application-defined key/value context (tenant ID, feature flag) across service boundaries
questions.explain: Baggage carries app context in-band; it is not automatically attached to spans, metrics or logs.

questions.q: A key caution when using Baggage:
options: It is encrypted, so debugging is hard
It is sent as plain-text headers to every downstream service - never put secrets or PII in it
questions.explain: Baggage travels with every hop, potentially to third parties; also mind cardinality if copied onto metrics.

questions.q: Why is BatchSpanProcessor preferred over SimpleSpanProcessor in production?
options: It exports asynchronously in batches with a bounded queue, so a slow exporter never blocks the app
questions.explain: SimpleSpanProcessor exports synchronously per span - fine for dev, dangerous in prod.

questions.q: Which sampler is the production standard for consistent whole-trace decisions plus a fixed root rate?
questions.explain: ParentBased honors the parent's decision; TraceIdRatioBased at the root gives a known rate; the decision rides in traceparent flags.

questions.q: 'Keep every trace with an error or >500 ms latency, sample 5% of the rest.' Where must this run?
options: Collector tail_sampling processor - only tail sampling sees whole-trace properties
questions.explain: Final latency and status do not exist at span start, so head sampling cannot act on them.

questions.q: OTLP over plain HTTP for traces uses, by default:
questions.explain: OTLP/HTTP: 4318 with /v1/traces, /v1/metrics, /v1/logs. 4317 is OTLP/gRPC.

questions.q: An app exits right after its last request and recent spans never arrive. Most likely fix?
options: Call shutdown()/forceFlush() on the providers so batched data is exported before exit
questions.explain: Batched telemetry sits in in-memory queues; without shutdown/flush it is lost on exit.

questions.q: What is an instrumentation scope?
options: The Kubernetes namespace of the workload
The name+version identity (typically of a library) passed to getTracer/getMeter, grouping the telemetry it emits
A firewall rule for the Collector
questions.explain: tracer = getTracer("shop.checkout", "1.4.2") sets the scope; in OTLP data is grouped Resource -> Scope -> records.

questions.q: Which environment variable turns the whole SDK into a no-op (kill switch)?
questions.explain: OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true disables the SDK entirely; a sampler of always_off would still leave metrics and logs active.

questions.q: What is the default limit for the number of attributes on a single span?
questions.explain: Span limits (default 128 attributes, plus configurable event/link counts and value lengths) protect the SDK from runaway memory.

questions.q: recordException(e) on a span does what?
options: Sets the span status to OK
Adds a timestamped 'exception' span event with exception details
Sends the exception to the Collector immediately
questions.explain: recordException adds an exception event; setting status=ERROR is a separate, explicit call.

questions.q: In the OTLP payload hierarchy, spans are grouped as:
questions.explain: Data is grouped first by Resource, then by InstrumentationScope, then the records - same shape for metrics and logs.

questions.q: What is the default metrics export interval of the PeriodicExportingMetricReader?
questions.explain: 60000 ms by default, changeable via OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL.

questions.q: How does the Prometheus exporter in the SDK differ from the OTLP metrics exporter?
options: It exposes an HTTP endpoint that Prometheus scrapes (pull), instead of pushing
questions.explain: OTLP metrics are pushed on an interval; the Prometheus exporter is pull/scrape-based with cumulative temporality.

questions.q: For work scheduled onto another thread or task, trace continuity requires:
options: Capturing the current Context when scheduling and restoring it inside the worker
questions.explain: Context is thread-/async-local; capture-and-restore is the standard pattern for background work.

questions.q: What does the tracestate header carry?
options: Vendor-/participant-specific key-value tracing state alongside traceparent
questions.explain: tracestate lets tracing systems attach their own state to the W3C context; the sampled bit lives in traceparent flags.

questions.q: In a Collector pipeline, what is the correct data flow?
questions.explain: Receivers get data in, processors transform it in an ordered chain, exporters send it out. That chain is a pipeline, one per signal type.

questions.q: What distinguishes a Connector from a Processor?
options: Connectors run outside the data path
A connector acts as an exporter in one pipeline and a receiver in another, and may change signal type
questions.explain: Connectors bridge pipelines (e.g. spans -> metrics via spanmetrics); processors stay inside one pipeline.

questions.q: Which component category is NOT on the telemetry data path?
questions.explain: Extensions (health_check, pprof, zpages, file_storage, auth) add side capabilities without touching data.

questions.q: Why must memory_limiter be the first processor?
options: So it can refuse data before downstream processors allocate more memory under pressure
questions.explain: Placed later it cannot prevent the OOM it exists to stop. When it trips, receivers return errors upstream (backpressure).

questions.q: Where does the batch processor belong in the chain?
questions.explain: Batch last, so only surviving, fully-enriched data is batched. Canonical order: memory_limiter -> enrichment -> filter/transform -> batch.

questions.q: A receiver is defined under receivers: but telemetry never arrives. Config is valid YAML. Most likely cause?
options: The receiver is not referenced in any pipeline under service.pipelines
questions.explain: Defining a component only declares it; it activates when listed in a service.pipelines entry. Classic trick question.

questions.q: Which processor attaches pod, namespace and deployment metadata in Kubernetes?
questions.explain: k8sattributes queries the K8s API and attaches k8s.pod.name, k8s.namespace.name, deployment, node as resource attributes.

questions.q: Which pair makes an exporter's queued data survive Collector restarts?
options: sending_queue with a file_storage extension as its storage
questions.explain: sending_queue.storage: file_storage persists the queue to disk; retry_on_failure alone is memory-only and lost on restart.

questions.q: Difference between otelcol (core) and otelcol-contrib?
options: Core is paid, contrib is free
Contrib bundles many community receivers/processors/exporters beyond the minimal stable core set
questions.explain: Contrib adds prometheus, kafka, k8sattributes, tail_sampling, vendor exporters and much more.

questions.q: What is the OpenTelemetry Collector Builder (OCB) for?
options: Compiling a custom Collector binary containing only the components you select
questions.explain: A custom distribution means a smaller binary and smaller attack surface.

questions.q: Which deployment pattern is the most common production topology?
options: Agent (per host/pod) chained to a central Gateway tier
questions.explain: Agents give local enrichment and a fast export target; the gateway centralizes auth, tail sampling, routing and fan-out.

questions.q: You scale Collector replicas horizontally and tail sampling starts making wrong decisions. Why?
options: Spans of one trace now land on different replicas, so no replica sees the whole trace
Sampling only works with one exporter
questions.explain: tail_sampling is stateful: it needs every span of a trace on the same instance.

questions.q: The standard fix for scattered traces with tail sampling is:
options: A front tier using the loadbalancing exporter (routing_key: traceID) sending to a back tier that runs tail_sampling
Sticky HTTP sessions on the app LB
questions.explain: Consistent hashing on TraceId guarantees all spans of a trace hit the same back-tier instance. Same idea applies to spanmetrics (often keyed on service).

questions.q: Which connector derives RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) from spans?
questions.explain: spanmetrics emits request counts, error counts and duration histograms from spans; servicegraph builds topology edge metrics.

questions.q: Which language do the transform and filter processors use for statements like delete_key(attributes, "http.user_agent")?
questions.explain: OTTL statements run against contexts (resource, scope, span, spanevent, metric, datapoint, log).

questions.q: Which receiver would you use to ingest log files written to disk by a legacy application?
questions.explain: The filelog receiver tails and parses files - the standard path for logs from apps you cannot instrument.

questions.q: The Collector's prometheus receiver works by:
options: Scraping Prometheus-format /metrics endpoints (pull), like Prometheus itself
questions.explain: Receivers can be push- or pull-based; the prometheus receiver pulls scrape targets. prometheusremotewrite is the push EXPORTER counterpart.

questions.q: Which exporter pushes metrics into a Prometheus-compatible backend rather than exposing a scrape endpoint?
questions.explain: prometheus (exporter) exposes an endpoint to be scraped; prometheusremotewrite actively pushes.

questions.q: Which processor performs head-style percentage sampling at the Collector?
questions.explain: probabilistic_sampler samples by percentage without buffering whole traces; tail_sampling is the policy-based whole-trace option.

questions.q: The OpenTelemetry Operator's OpenTelemetryCollector CRD supports which deployment modes?
questions.explain: Four modes; the Instrumentation CRD separately auto-injects language agents via pod annotations.

questions.q: In Kubernetes, which Operator feature shards Prometheus scrape targets across Collector replicas?
questions.explain: The TargetAllocator distributes scrape targets so the (stateful) prometheus receiver can scale horizontally.

questions.q: Using a Collector between apps and backends gives all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Automatic code instrumentation of the application
questions.explain: The Collector processes telemetry in transit; generating telemetry is the job of SDKs, instrumentation libraries and agents.

questions.q: Which OTTL statement redacts an API key inside url.full?
questions.explain: replace_pattern does regex substitution in the transform processor - the canonical in-pipeline redaction example.

questions.q: Multiple pipelines for the same signal type in one Collector are:
options: Allowed, using named pipelines like traces/tenant-a and traces/tenant-b
Only possible with two Collector binaries
questions.explain: type/name syntax applies to pipelines and components; one receiver can feed many pipelines and exporters can be shared.

questions.q: Quickest way to verify what telemetry a Collector is actually receiving?
options: Add the debug exporter to the pipeline and watch stdout
questions.explain: The debug exporter (successor to the deprecated logging exporter; verbosity basic/normal/detailed) prints incoming data - the fastest ground truth.

questions.q: Rising otelcol_exporter_send_failed_spans plus a growing sending queue most likely indicates:
options: The downstream backend is unreachable or unhealthy; the exporter is retrying
questions.explain: exporter_send_failed_* + queue growth = outbound trouble; retries and (persistent) queues absorb it until the backend recovers.

questions.q: otelcol_processor_refused_spans is climbing during a traffic spike. Most likely source?
options: memory_limiter rejecting data because memory crossed its threshold
questions.explain: processor_refused/dropped_* under load is typically memory_limiter shedding; backpressure propagates to senders via receiver errors.

questions.q: Which extension provides liveness/readiness endpoints for Kubernetes probes?
questions.explain: health_check (default :13133). pprof (:1777) = Go profiling; zpages (:55679) = live debug pages.

questions.q: By default, where can Prometheus scrape the Collector's own internal metrics?
questions.explain: Self-metrics default to :8888. 4317 = OTLP/gRPC ingest, 13133 = health_check, 55679 = zpages.

questions.q: A trace shows services A and C but B's spans are missing; B's SDK logs show exporter timeouts. Best first step?
options: Check B's OTLP endpoint/port/protocol configuration and network reachability to its Collector
questions.explain: Exporter timeouts point to connectivity/config: endpoint, 4317 vs 4318, grpc vs http/protobuf, TLS, network policy.

questions.q: To see the SDK's own diagnostic output (exporter errors, retries) you set:
questions.explain: OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug (or the language equivalent) surfaces the SDK's internal logging. Adding a console exporter confirms data is produced at all.

questions.q: An exporter receives HTTP 401 from the backend. How is this error class handled?
options: Treated as permanent and dropped without retry - fix credentials
questions.explain: 4xx auth/format errors are permanent (retrying cannot help); 5xx/timeouts are transient and retried with exponential backoff.

questions.q: Which zpages page shows live traces flowing through the Collector itself?
questions.explain: zpages serves HTML debug pages such as /debug/tracez and pipeline/receiver/exporter activity views on :55679.

questions.q: What does the schema_url attached to a Resource or instrumentation scope tell a consumer?
options: The network endpoint the telemetry was exported to
Which version of the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions the producer's attribute names follow
A checksum used to detect corrupted OTLP payloads
The URL of the backend's query API
questions.explain: schema_url pins the semantic-convention version the producer used, so consumers can apply schema transformations to normalize attribute names across producers running different versions.

questions.q: A histogram's cardinality explodes right after a release. Where can you cut it WITHOUT redeploying the applications?
options: Only by editing and redeploying the application code
In the Collector, using the transform or attributes processor to drop or hash the offending attribute key
By switching the exporter from OTLP to Prometheus
By moving the memory_limiter processor to the end of the chain
questions.explain: The Collector's transform/attributes processors remove or hash high-cardinality keys in transit, so no app redeploy is needed. The durable fix is an SDK View at the source once you can ship the apps.

questions.q: All three OpenTelemetry signals follow the same provider pattern. What is the correct sequence?
options: Provider and Component are created independently and joined by the SDK
Provider creates Component, which produces Data
Data is registered with a Component, which registers with a Provider
Component creates Provider, which produces Data
questions.explain: TracerProvider -> Tracer -> spans, MeterProvider -> Meter -> measurements, LoggerProvider -> Logger -> log records. The provider is the SDK entry point you configure; it hands out the component that actually emits data.

questions.q: A span represents work happening entirely inside your own process, with no network boundary crossed. Which SpanKind?
questions.explain: INTERNAL is the default and covers in-process work. CLIENT/SERVER are the two sides of a synchronous remote call; PRODUCER/CONSUMER the two sides of asynchronous messaging.

questions.q: During a request your code retries a failed database call three times. Each retry takes roughly 200 ms and can fail independently. How should each attempt be represented?
options: As a span link per attempt
As an attribute counting the retries
As a span event per attempt
As a child span per attempt
questions.explain: Each attempt has its own duration and its own success/failure, so it is a unit of work: a child span. Span events are point-in-time markers with no duration; links connect spans in different traces.

questions.q: Which of these belongs on the Resource rather than on a span?
questions.explain: A Resource describes the entity producing telemetry and is constant for the process lifetime. deployment.environment.name is a property of the deployment; the others vary per request.

questions.q: Which attribute would be most dangerous to add to a metric?
questions.explain: order.id is unbounded: every order creates a new time series. The others have small, bounded value sets. Unbounded metric attributes cause cardinality explosion; put identifiers on spans and logs instead.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the semantic convention stability levels?
questions.explain: Semantic conventions are marked Experimental (may change), Stable (backwards-compatibility guaranteed) or Deprecated. 'Provisional' is not an OpenTelemetry stability level.

questions.q: A span finishes successfully and instrumentation touches nothing. What is its status?
questions.explain: Unset is the default and means 'no explicit judgement was made' - not a failure. Ok must be set deliberately by application code; Error is set by instrumentation on a known failure. There is no 'Success' status.

questions.q: A log record needs to be correlated with the exact operation that produced it. Which field does that?
questions.explain: TraceId ties the record to the whole request; SpanId narrows it to the individual operation within that request. Both are first-class fields on the LogRecord.

questions.q: Which signal best answers 'what proportion of requests to this endpoint exceeded 500 ms in the last hour'?
options: Traces, by counting spans over the period
Logs, by parsing durations from the message body
questions.explain: A histogram aggregates every request into buckets cheaply and is unaffected by sampling. Traces are usually sampled, so counting spans gives a biased proportion; parsing logs is expensive and lossy.

questions.q: You need to report total bytes written by the process, read from a counter in /proc on a timer. Which instrument?
questions.explain: The value is monotonically increasing and is read at collection time rather than incremented per event, so it is an asynchronous monotonic sum: ObservableCounter. A plain Counter would require you to compute and add deltas yourself.

questions.q: Which OTLP point type does an UpDownCounter produce?
questions.explain: UpDownCounter values are additive but can decrease, so it emits a Sum with is_monotonic false. Counter emits a Sum with is_monotonic true; Gauge instruments emit Gauge points.

questions.q: Aggregation temporality is a property of which point types?
questions.explain: Only aggregated point types carry temporality, because only they cover a time window: Sum and Histogram (including exponential histograms). A Gauge is a single instantaneous value, so delta vs cumulative is meaningless for it.

questions.q: Which component owns the temporality preference?
questions.explain: The spec says the temporality function SHOULD be obtained from the exporter - the backend decides what it can ingest (Prometheus wants cumulative, several SaaS backends prefer delta). The MetricReader picks it up from its exporter and applies it.

questions.q: You want the same metrics exported to two backends, one preferring delta and one cumulative. What do you configure?
options: Two MetricReaders, each with its own exporter and preference
One exporter with two temporality settings
questions.explain: A MetricReader owns exactly one exporter and one temporality preference. Register two readers on the same MeterProvider and each performs its own collection with its own temporality.

questions.q: You want spans exported to both a production backend and a local console. What do you configure?
options: Two span processors, each owning one exporter
One exporter configured with two endpoints
questions.explain: A span processor wraps exactly one exporter. Register multiple processors on the TracerProvider - typically a BatchSpanProcessor for the backend and a SimpleSpanProcessor for the console.

questions.q: In a SpanProcessor, at which hook is the span mutable?
questions.explain: OnStart receives a writable span, which is how processors enrich spans (for example a baggage span processor copying baggage onto attributes). By OnEnd the span is read-only.

questions.q: How does an exporter get attached to a TracerProvider?
options: Via the Tracer, at span creation
Via a global registry keyed by signal type
It is passed to a span processor, which the provider holds
questions.explain: The provider knows only about span processors; each processor owns an exporter. That indirection is what lets you choose batching vs simple export, and to fan out to several exporters.

questions.q: A View is registered with a Drop aggregation matching an instrument. What happens?
options: The instrument is renamed and exported separately
Measurements are discarded and nothing is exported for that instrument
Data points are exported with a value of zero
The View is rejected at registration
questions.explain: Drop tells the SDK to ignore all measurements for the matching instrument - the standard way to switch off a noisy metric without touching application code.

questions.q: A View's attribute filter is configured. How does it behave?
options: It is an allow-list - only the named keys are kept
It applies only to asynchronous instruments
It is a deny-list - the named keys are removed
questions.explain: attribute_keys is an allow-list: the listed keys MUST be kept and everything else is dropped. Getting this backwards is a classic way to accidentally throw away every dimension you cared about.

questions.q: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME is set to 'api'. OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES contains service.name=web and team=platform. What is the resulting resource?
options: The configuration is rejected as conflicting
questions.explain: The spec is explicit: if service.name is also provided in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, OTEL_SERVICE_NAME takes precedence. The other attributes in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES are unaffected.

questions.q: Order these from highest precedence to lowest for resource attributes.
options: Environment variables, code, SDK default, resource detectors
Code, environment variables, resource detectors, SDK default
SDK default, resource detectors, environment variables, code
Resource detectors, code, environment variables, SDK default
questions.explain: Explicit wins over implicit: attributes set in code beat OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, which beats what resource detectors discover, which beats the SDK's built-in defaults (such as service.name=unknown_service).

questions.q: What is the default value of OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER?
questions.explain: The default is parentbased_always_on: honour the parent's decision if there is one, otherwise sample every root span. Nothing is dropped until you configure a ratio.

questions.q: A service is configured ParentBased(root=TraceIdRatioBased(0.1)). A request arrives with traceparent flags 00. What happens?
options: The span is sampled with 10% probability
The span is sampled with 1% probability
questions.explain: Flags 00 means the remote parent was not sampled, so ParentBased applies remote_parent_not_sampled (AlwaysOff) and drops the span. The root delegate only runs when there is no parent - that is what keeps traces whole.

questions.q: A service is configured with a bare traceidratio sampler, arg 0.5. A request arrives with traceparent flags 01. What happens?
options: The span is always sampled, because the parent was sampled
50% chance, decided from the trace ID; the parent flag is ignored
questions.explain: TraceIdRatioBased on its own ignores the parent entirely and hashes the trace ID. Because the hash is deterministic, all services with the same ratio agree - but mix ratios and you get broken traces. Wrap it in ParentBased to be safe.

questions.q: A span has trace flags 00 but IsRecording() returns true. What does this mean?
options: It is a no-op span from the API
It is buffered and will be exported on the next flush
It collects data locally but will not be exported
questions.explain: This is the RECORD_ONLY sampling result: the span records attributes and events (so in-process consumers such as span-to-metrics can use it) but the sampled flag stays off, so it is not propagated as sampled and not exported.

questions.q: Baggage is set at your ingress service. Do downstream spans carry those entries as attributes?
options: Yes, but only for entries under 32 bytes
Only if a baggage span processor or explicit code copies them
No, and there is no configuration that would make it so
questions.explain: Baggage propagates across services in a header, but it never becomes span attributes by itself. You opt in - via a baggage span processor or by reading baggage in code - which is deliberate, since baggage often holds sensitive values.

questions.q: Three propagators are configured. What happens on inject?
options: One is chosen based on the outbound content type
questions.explain: A composite propagator runs every configured propagator on both inject and extract, so the outbound request carries all their headers at once. That is how you bridge a fleet that is half W3C and half B3.

questions.q: An application uses the OpenTelemetry API with no SDK registered. What does tracer.startSpan() return?
options: Null, which the caller must handle
A non-recording span carrying the parent's SpanContext
A recording span buffered until an SDK registers
A span with a freshly generated trace ID
questions.explain: The API's no-op implementation never returns null and never throws - it returns a non-recording span that still carries the current SpanContext, so context propagation keeps working through uninstrumented hops.

questions.q: Who is the API's no-op default implementation primarily designed for?
options: Library authors instrumenting without imposing a dependency
Application developers who forget to configure an SDK
The Collector, which can then skip parsing
questions.explain: A library can depend on the API alone and ship native instrumentation. If the application never configures an SDK, the calls compile to near-zero-cost no-ops - so nobody pays for telemetry they did not ask for.

questions.q: Which instrumentation approach requires no change to the application's deployment artifact?
questions.explain: Zero-code instrumentation attaches at startup - a -javaagent flag, a Python launcher, an operator-injected init container - so the same binary or image ships unchanged. Instrumentation libraries still have to be added as dependencies.

questions.q: How does the OpenTelemetry Java agent instrument an application?
options: By requiring each library to instrument itself
questions.explain: The agent hooks the JVM's class loading and rewrites bytecode as classes are loaded, so supported frameworks are instrumented without a source change or rebuild.

questions.q: A process using a BatchSpanProcessor is killed without Shutdown() being called. What is lost?
options: Nothing - the SDK flushes automatically on exit
Every span still sitting in the processor's queue
Only spans whose previous export attempt failed
Only the most recently exported batch
questions.explain: The queue lives in process memory and is only drained on the schedule or by Shutdown()/ForceFlush(). Kill the process and everything queued goes with it - which is why graceful shutdown handling matters for short-lived jobs and serverless.

questions.q: In the log data model, where do TraceId and SpanId live?
options: Inside the Body, for the backend to parse
As top-level fields on the LogRecord
questions.explain: TraceId, SpanId and TraceFlags are first-class top-level fields of the LogRecord - not attributes and not text in the body - so correlation needs no parsing and no naming convention.

questions.q: Why does OpenTelemetry provide log appenders rather than a logging API for application developers?
options: Appenders are more performant than a native API
Logging APIs cannot carry trace context
Applications already have logging frameworks, so bridging beats replacing
The Logs specification was never finished
questions.explain: Unlike tracing and metrics, logging was a solved problem in every language. OTel therefore bridges existing frameworks (Logback, log4j, Serilog, Python logging) and adds trace context, instead of asking anyone to rewrite their logging calls.

questions.q: A processor is fully defined under processors: but referenced in no pipeline. What happens at startup?
options: It is applied to every pipeline by default
The Collector starts normally and the processor does nothing
It is applied to the first pipeline only
questions.explain: Defining a component only declares it. Components are enabled by listing them in a pipeline under service:, so an unreferenced definition is inert - a very common reason a processor 'is not working'.

questions.q: A pipeline lists a processor that is not defined anywhere in the config. What happens at startup?
options: The Collector starts and substitutes a default
The Collector fails to start with a configuration error
The Collector starts and skips the unknown processor
The Collector starts but marks that pipeline unhealthy
questions.explain: Configuration is validated before anything runs; a pipeline referencing an undefined component is a hard error. Nothing is silently defaulted or skipped - the opposite of the unreferenced-definition case.

questions.q: Which processor order is correct?
questions.explain: Two rules decide it: memory_limiter first so it can shed load before anything downstream buffers, and batch last because batching clears the request context that processors like k8sattributes depend on. (The full recommended order puts filtering/sampling right after memory_limiter, so you do not enrich data you are about to drop.)

questions.q: The memory_limiter crosses its soft limit. What does it do?
options: Forces garbage collection and continues accepting data
Drops the oldest data already in the pipeline
Refuses incoming data, returning a retryable error to receivers
Shuts the pipeline down until memory recovers
questions.explain: At the soft limit it refuses new data with a retryable error, pushing back on senders rather than discarding what is already in flight. Only at the hard limit does it force a garbage collection.

questions.q: You must remove one attribute from spans belonging to a single service, keeping the spans themselves. Which processor?
questions.explain: transform runs OTTL statements such as delete_key(attributes, "...") with a where clause on the service - it edits data in place. filter would drop the whole span, which is not what was asked.

questions.q: In OTTL, what does declaring 'context: span' establish?
options: Which collection is iterated, and what a bare 'attributes' reference resolves to
Read access downward into span events
That the statements apply only to trace pipelines
The order in which statements execute
questions.explain: The context sets the iteration scope and the meaning of unqualified paths: under 'span', attributes means span attributes, while resource.attributes must be qualified. Choose 'spanevent' and you iterate events instead.

questions.q: With error_mode set to propagate, what happens when an OTTL statement fails?
options: That statement is skipped and the rest continue
The entire payload batch is dropped
questions.explain: propagate returns the error upstream, so the whole payload is rejected - safe when correctness matters more than completeness. ignore skips the failing statement and silently continues; silent does the same without logging.

questions.q: Why must k8sattributes run on the agent Collector rather than a gateway?
options: It associates telemetry to pods using the connection's source IP
Resource attributes are immutable by the time data reaches a gateway
The processor only compiles into DaemonSet builds
Gateways cannot be granted Kubernetes API access
questions.explain: Pod identity is derived from the sending connection's IP. At a gateway that IP is the agent's, not the workload's, so every record would be attributed to the wrong pod.

questions.q: The Collector is started with several --config flags pointing at different files. How are they combined?
options: Only the last file is used
Concatenated in order and parsed as one YAML document
Each file becomes an independent pipeline
A deep merge, where later sources override earlier ones at each level
questions.explain: The confmap layer deep-merges all sources into one in-memory configuration, with later sources winning key by key. That is what lets a base config be overlaid with an environment-specific fragment.

questions.q: otelcol_exporter_queue_size has reached otelcol_exporter_queue_capacity. What does that indicate?
options: The queue is sized correctly for the load
The exporter cannot keep up and data is being dropped
questions.explain: A full sending queue means export is slower than ingest, and anything arriving after that is rejected. Look at backend latency or errors first; raising the queue size only buys time.

questions.q: Which metric tells you a Collector is rejecting data at ingestion?
questions.explain: receiver_refused_* counts data turned away at the front door - typically memory_limiter pushing back. Exporter failures are at the far end of the pipeline and processor drops are deliberate filtering.

questions.q: A config written in 2023 references the logging exporter. What happens on a current Collector?
options: It works, with a deprecation warning
It fails to start; logging was removed in favour of debug
It works only if the internal log level is set to debug
It silently falls back to the debug exporter
questions.explain: The logging exporter was deprecated in v0.86.0 and removed in v0.111.0. An unknown exporter type is a configuration error, so the Collector refuses to start - replace it with debug, which takes the same verbosity option.

questions.q: Three services each produce their own disconnected trace instead of one tree. Most likely cause?
options: The Collector batching spans from different services together
questions.explain: Broken parent-child linkage across services points at propagation: one side injects W3C while the other extracts B3, or an uninstrumented hop drops the header. Clock skew misaligns a trace's timings but keeps it one trace; batching never affects trace structure.

questions.q: Where does schema_url appear in an OTLP payload?
options: Once per request, at the top level
On the Resource and on the InstrumentationScope
questions.explain: schema_url sits at both levels, so a resource and an instrumentation library can declare different semantic-convention versions in the same payload - which is exactly what a consumer needs to apply schema transformations.
